explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Asaph says it three ways: "be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God." When you're this worried, one way to say it just isn't enough. I think he's asking God to speak up and act.

Nope, nothing about angry here. Asaph never asks God to hold anything back in that way. The three requests are "be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God." They all say the same thing: Asaph wants God to speak up and act.

Close in mood, friend, since Asaph is clearly in a hurry. But the word he uses isn't impatient. He says "be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God." Three ways of asking God not to stay quiet.

Yes, cunning. Asaph says "With cunning they scheme against Your people and conspire against those You cherish." Notice the words "those You cherish." Asaph calls them that, and it tells you whose people these are.

I get why you'd guess it, but fear isn't the word. Asaph says the enemies scheme "with cunning." That means they're sneaky and planning ahead, which is the opposite of scared. I'd rather not meet anyone who schemes like that.
Haste would be a rushed job, friend, and that's not what Asaph describes. He says they scheme "with cunning" against God's people. Sneaky planning, done carefully. Nothing about a hurry in the verse.

That's what they say, and it's a heavy one. Asaph quotes them: "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." It's not about a little trouble, it's about making Israel disappear. That's why Asaph is praying so hard.

Tribute is paying money to a stronger nation, and that's not what these enemies say. They want Israel gone. The quote is "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." That's a whole lot bigger than a payment.

The king never comes up in what they say, friend. Their words are about the whole nation: "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." They aren't aiming at one man, they want all of Israel erased.
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: "For with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You." These nations agree completely. That's what makes the plot so serious.

Right, it's false. Asaph says "with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You." They're not arguing over the plan, they're all in on it. A group that agrees that much is a problem.

Yes, and look at the wording. Asaph says "they form an alliance against You," and he's talking to God. So the alliance is against God Himself. Asaph didn't see this as only a fight over land and borders.
No king is named in this verse, friend. Asaph speaks to God and says "they form an alliance against You." The "You" is God. So the alliance is against Him.
The high priest doesn't show up anywhere in this psalm. Asaph is praying to God, and he says "they form an alliance against You." That "You" is God Himself. Nobody else gets named as the target.

explanations.answer: Defeat them like He defeated those enemies
explanations.explanation: That's it. Asaph prays "Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon." He's pointing at times God already came through and asking for the same again. Smart move, bringing the history into his prayer.
Servants never come up, friend. Asaph says "Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon." He's asking God to defeat today's enemies the way He defeated those ones.

explanations.answer: Send them back to their own lands
explanations.explanation: Sending them home isn't the request. Asaph says "Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon." Those enemies were defeated, and he's asking for the same to be done to the ones plotting now.

Yes, the pastures of God. Asaph quotes them as saying "Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God." Those four Midianite leaders wanted what belonged to God. They'd have done better to ask for a cookie.
Nice tree, but it's not in this verse. Asaph quotes them as saying "Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God." The thing they wanted was God's pastures.
Gold sounds like a good guess, friend, but it isn't here. The quote is "Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God." They wanted pastures, and Asaph says they were God's.
Correct. Asaph prays, "Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind." Chaff is the light stuff that blows away and doesn't stay put. He's asking for the plotters to be scattered.
It's actually true, friend. Asaph prays, "Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind." Chaff is light and the wind takes it right off. That's the picture he asks for.

Yes, His tempest. Asaph says "so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm." After the fire on the mountains, he asks for wind and storm to chase them. Two pictures, same prayer.
Hailstones are stormy, so I see the thinking. But Asaph never mentions them. He says "so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm." The word is tempest.
No armies in this verse, friend. Asaph asks God to "pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm." He keeps it to the weather, and the answer is tempest.

That's the surprise, and you caught it. Asaph asks God to cover their faces with shame "that they may seek Your name, O LORD." The prayer isn't only about them being stopped. It also asks that they would look for the LORD.

I can see why you'd expect it, since the prayer is pretty intense. But look at what it says: "that they may seek Your name, O LORD." The word is seek. Asaph wants them looking for God, not cursing Him.
Forget sounds natural after all that shame, friend. But the verse says "that they may seek Your name, O LORD." The word is seek. Asaph is asking that they'd look for God.

Not quite. Right after asking that they seek God's name, Asaph says "May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace." So he keeps going. Both prayers sit side by side in the psalm.

Right, it's false. Asaph follows with "May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace." He doesn't stop asking after he mentions seeking God's name. Both requests are in his prayer, and I think that's a lot to hold at once.

explanations.answer: That the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the last line, and what a finish. Asaph prays, "May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth." The whole psalm ends on who God is. Everything else in the prayer leads up to that.

explanations.answer: That Israel will rule over every nation on earth
explanations.explanation: Israel ruling isn't where Asaph lands, friend. His last line is "May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth." He ends with who God is, not with what Israel will do.

explanations.answer: That Asaph's prayers are always heard in heaven
explanations.explanation: Asaph never makes it about himself here. He ends with "May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth." The last words are about the LORD, and that's where the psalm finishes.
